concept.name: Unemployment rate
concept.definition: The percentage of the civilian labor force that is jobless, actively seeking work, and available to take a job. In the United States it is estimated monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics from the Current Population Survey of about 60,000 households and published in The Employment Situation report.
concept.intuition: It is the best-known single gauge of labor-market slack: a low rate means most people who want work have it, while a rising rate signals a weakening economy.
concept.mechanics: BLS divides the number of unemployed - people with no job who actively searched in the prior four weeks and are available for work, plus those awaiting recall from layoff - by the labor force (employed plus unemployed). Data come from live Census Bureau interviews covering the week containing the 12th of the month, are weighted to population estimates, and are seasonally adjusted.
concept.formula: Unemployment rate = (Number unemployed / Civilian labor force) x 100, where the labor force = employed + unemployed.
concept.failure_modes: It excludes discouraged workers who stopped searching, so slack is understated when participation falls; the headline U-3 rate is also revised and can diverge from broader underutilization measures like U-6 during stress.
concept.misconceptions: It is not derived from unemployment-insurance claims - BLS notes UI records cover only about one-third of the unemployed - and it counts as unemployed only people actively searching or awaiting recall, not everyone without a job.
concept.example: In April 2020 the U.S. unemployment rate jumped from 4.4% in March to 14.7%, the highest in the series' history, as pandemic lockdowns idled over 20 million workers.

citations.source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, How the Government Measures Unemployment
